query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Tailored thermomechanical processing that refines the inherited lamellar structure into an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure in eutectic high-entropy alloys (specifically AlCoCrFeNi2.1) will simultaneously increase tensile strength and ductility relative to the as‐cast state.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy (AlCoCrFeNi2.1) with a conventional as-cast coarse lamellar microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled rolling procedure followed by an optimized intermediate-temperature annealing treatment to transform the coarse lamellar microstructure into an ultrafine-grained duplex (composite) microstructure.
generation.conditions: Processing under conditions near, but below, the eutectic temperature to retain the lamellar architecture, with subsequent annealing at a temperature that promotes grain refinement without significant coarsening; tests conducted at room temperature under uniaxial tension.
generation.structural_mediator: An ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that retains the inherited lamellar features, enabling two-hierarchical constraints and microcrack-arresting mechanisms.
generation.mechanism: The refined structure enhances the work hardening capability by imposing a two-scale constraint on deformation, which simultaneously promotes strength (due to grain refinement and dislocation accumulation) and ductility (via enhanced strain accommodation and microcrack arrest mechanisms).
generation.predicted_outcome: The ultrafine-grained duplex alloy will exhibit higher yield strength and greater elongation at failure compared to the as-cast alloy, indicative of an improved strength–ductility synergy.
generation.baseline: The as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with a coarse lamellar microstructure showing standard mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: This outcome is expected in eutectic high-entropy alloys similar in composition to AlCoCrFeNi2.1 when processed under the specified thermal and mechanical conditions at room temperature during uniaxial tensile testing.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvement in mechanical properties is uncertain and may depend on fine details of the processing parameters; further optimization might be required to standardize the improvement.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy samples: one set processed by the proposed controlled rolling and annealing to achieve the ultrafine-grained duplex structure, and another set using conventional as-cast processing. Characterize the microstructure using SEM/TEM and then perform standardized room temperature uniaxial tensile tests.
measurements: Grain size and phase distribution via microstructural analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the processed samples do not show statistically significant increases in both yield strength and ductility (elongation) relative to the as-cast samples, or if the microstructure fails to exhibit the expected duplex features, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Enhanced strength–ductility synergy in ultrafine-grained eutectic high-entropy alloys by inheriting microstructural lamellae

Abstract: Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism.
